I will explain the problem, how the system works, what it found, and how I tested it. One point I will repeat: the optimization results are a what-if simulation, not real savings.

The certificate on the right was issued on 25 July 2026. The project I will present was the single integrated project of this internship.
3: Unified Mentor Pvt. Ltd. is a mentorship and training organisation that offers remote internships. Its Corporate Identity Number and its ISO 9001:2015 statement are printed on my certificate. I have not stated the company's founding year or history, because I could not confirm them from an official source. 4: Nassau Candy makes 15 products at 5 factories and ships across the United States and Canada. The company asked three things: how good are the current routes, what looks irregular, and could a different factory allocation shorten the distance. The hard part is on the right. The data has no usable shipping times, no factory column, no customer coordinates and no cost or capacity data. So I labelled every number as dataset, calculated or assumption.
5: These were my six objectives, in the order of the work: prepare the data, measure distance and score routes, build the linear-programming model, detect anomalies and make recommendations, present everything in a dashboard with reports, and test it. On the right, in scope is one dataset analysed locally. Out of scope is anything about deployment, delivery-time prediction, cost modelling or machine learning.
6: The data is one CSV file, Nassau Candy Distributor, with 10,194 order lines and 18 columns. There are 8,549 orders, 5,044 customers, 15 products and 59 states and provinces. The factory count of 5 comes from a product-to-factory map in the project brief, so that part is an assumption. Standard Class is the most used ship mode at 60 percent. I recomputed all these statistics from the unmodified file.
7: The system is written in Python. Pandas and NumPy handle the data, Streamlit and Plotly build the dashboard, Google OR-Tools solves the optimization with its GLOP solver, ReportLab and OpenPyXL create the PDF and Excel reports, and pytest runs the tests. These are the exact versions in the project's own virtual environment. It runs locally only; it is not deployed.
9: The loader, load and clean, is the first step for every page. It has nine ordered steps: check the file, convert Sales and Units to numbers, drop invalid rows, trim text, parse the dates, compute a raw lead time for display only, map each product to its factory and each state to its centroid, compute the haversine distance, and flag repeated order lines. On this dataset 10,194 rows go in and 10,194 come out. Nothing is deleted, and an unknown value is never turned into zero.
10: Route analytics has two parts. First, the haversine formula gives the straight-line distance on a sphere from a factory to the centre of a state. For example, Wicked Choccy's to Texas is 971.5 miles. Second, the Route Efficiency Score is 70 percent distance score plus 30 percent ship-mode score. The weights and the ship-mode values are my assumptions, and they are editable in the dashboard. The worked example gives 71.25. Because shipping dates are unusable, this is a proxy and not a delivery-time measure.
11: The optimization model asks one question: if other factories could make a product, how much shorter would the total distance be? Demand is grouped into 383 cells, each a state or province and a product. The model decides how many units of each cell come from each factory, to minimise units times miles. Every cell's demand must be met, and capacity and eligibility are optional limits. It is a transportation problem solved with Google OR-Tools GLOP, which uses the simplex method. Because of its structure the answer comes out in whole numbers. All of it is hypothetical, because capacities and eligibility are my assumptions.
12: The Scenario Simulator lets the user compare two to four what-if scenarios with the existing allocation. A scenario is a name, an eligibility rule, an optional capacity headroom and an optional cost rate. The table shows the four runs I verified. With no capacity limits the distance falls 58.8 percent, but that is an upper bound. Keeping each factory at its current volume gives 43 percent, and with 20 percent headroom 48.9 percent. The last row is a control: allowing only the current mapping gives exactly the existing 48,099,961, which shows the model is consistent. None of this is a real saving.
13: Anomaly detection uses simple statistics, mainly the interquartile range, plus consistency rules. It only flags records for review and never deletes or changes anything. The single outlier is a very long, low-volume route to Newfoundland and Labrador. The 3,018 repeated lines need a decision by the data owner. Recommendations are simple if-then rules. Each shows the reason, the exact rule, the supporting numbers, a basis label and a priority. There are 17: 9 high, 4 medium and 4 low. No machine learning is used. Eight of them are hypothetical.
14: These are real screenshots of the running dashboard, with no editing. It has eight pages that share one sidebar of filters: Executive Overview, Geographic Analysis, Route Performance, Optimization Center, Scenario Simulator, Smart Recommendations, Anomaly Detection and Reports. I opened every page in a real browser with no errors and checked all 23 download buttons. In the viva I can show any page live. Every hypothetical page carries a warning banner.
8: This is the architecture, in four layers. The data layer is the read-only CSV, loaded and cleaned by route_core.py, with my editable assumptions in config.py. The calculation layer is seven modules with no Streamlit code, so they can be tested without a browser. The amber ones, optimization and scenarios, are the hypothetical simulation modules. The interface layer is the app shell, shared helpers and the eight pages, and the report generator writes the PDF, Excel and CSV files. The key rule: Streamlit code lives only in app.py, ui and views.
15: Here are the main results. On the left is the hypothetical distance comparison. The existing allocation is about 48.1 million unit-miles. The simulation shows 43 percent less if each factory keeps its current volume, 48.9 percent with 20 percent headroom, and 58.8 percent with no limits. The last one is an upper bound and not a plan, because it would load the three small factories 7 to 16 times more than today, as shown on the right. On the right top are calculated route scores: the best route is 74.6 and the worst is 16.1. I want to stress that no allocation was implemented and no saving has been realised.
16: I treated testing as part of the design. There are 268 automated tests in 15 files, and all 268 passed in each of four environments, including one with the oldest package versions the project supports. I also opened all eight pages in a real browser and checked 23 downloads. The tests protect the original data file, the product map and the worked examples. To be honest about limits: the continuous-integration file has never been run, the Excel file was checked by reading it back and not by opening it in Excel, and I did not measure coverage or run a user survey.
17: From this project I learned the full chain from raw data to decision support. On the left are the skills, each backed by a part of the system. On the right are the main challenges and how I handled them. The biggest lesson is that the data decides what you can honestly claim. Because the shipping dates were unusable, I built a clearly labelled proxy score instead of inventing a delivery-time metric.
18: To conclude: in one month I built a single integrated system that cleans the data, measures distances, scores routes, solves an optimization model, compares scenarios, flags anomalies, makes explainable recommendations and generates reports, with 268 tests. The optimization results are hypothetical, there are no operational outcomes, and the limitations are stated in the report. For future work, the most valuable step is to replace my assumptions with real eligibility, capacity and cost data. Thank you. I am happy to take questions.
